docs.title: Hostel Room Swap Service
docs.text:
Author(s):

  • Aabhas Khandelwal, CSED, 1024030673
  • Aakash Chawla, CSED, 1024031097
  • Joy Soni, CSED, 1024030674

Group 3C51, under Dr. Raghav B. Venkataramaiyer.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Students are allocated hostel rooms they did not ask for -- wrong hostel, wrong floor, wrong roommate, wrong room type. Direct one-to-one swaps rarely work, because two students hardly ever want exactly what the other has.

A three-way rotation usually does work: A takes B's room, B takes C's, C takes A's. Nobody can find those chains by hand across a few thousand rooms.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Students submit weighted preferences over hostel, floor, direction, attached washroom, room type and roommate, marking any of them as hard or soft. The service returns up to three swap options, each with a match percentage and the list of preferences it does and does not meet.

The three options differ in kind, not just in score:

Option Best at Best overall match highest average satisfaction Fastest to execute shortest chain, fewest approvals Best location fit hostel, floor and direction

An option is only labelled with one of these if it genuinely beats the others on that measure, so sometimes fewer than three are shown.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
The pool is closed: the only rooms available are the ones the participants already hold. So a solution is a permutation of students over bed slots, and the swap chains are that permutation's cycles.

  • Hungarian algorithm (scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment) over a students x slots cost matrix finds the best permutation.
  • Murty's algorithm enumerates the next best ones, which matters because the optimal assignment often makes somebody worse off and gets rejected.
  • A feasibility layer keeps only chains where nobody loses and at least one student gains.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
pip install -e "./code[dev]"
pytest -q
uvicorn hostelswap.api:app --reload

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Without DATABASE_URL the app serves a built-in demo cohort, so no database is needed to try it.

To work on the web UI, run the Vite dev server next to the API. It proxies /api to port 8000:

npm --prefix frontend install
npm --prefix frontend run dev

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
• Matching engine, fairness filter and ranking: done, unit-tested.
  • Swap rounds: enroll, set priorities, lock, run, offer chains, respond, execute.
  • FastAPI backend with student and admin logins, on Postgres (Supabase), with schema migrations in db/migrations/.
  • React + TypeScript web UI for students and admins.
  • 137 tests passing.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Generated from the app's OpenAPI schema. Interactive docs, always in step with the code, are served by every running server at /docs, for example https://hostelswap.aakashchawla.space/docs. Requests and responses are JSON. The session is an httpOnly cookie set by POST /api/auth/login. Errors: 401 not signed in, 403 wrong role, 404 no such item, 409 not allowed in the current state, 503 no database configured.

docs.text:
Requires: None for login; a session for the rest.

Method Path Purpose Body / query POST /api/auth/login Sign in with a roll number or email; sets the session cookie. identifier: string, password: string POST /api/auth/logout Sign out; deletes the session. GET /api/auth/me The signed-in user and their role.

docs.title: Student
docs.text:
Requires: A student session.

Method Path Purpose Body / query GET /api/student/room The student's current room and bed. GET /api/student/round The current round for the student's hostel and whether they are enrolled. POST /api/student/round/{round_id}/enroll Join or leave an open round. enrolled: boolean GET /api/student/round/{round_id}/room-types Room types the student may ask for in this round. GET /api/student/round/{round_id}/priorities The student's saved priorities. PUT /api/student/round/{round_id}/priorities Replace the student's priorities (open rounds only). priorities: list of PriorityItem GET /api/student/round/{round_id}/roommate Roommate request sent, and requests received. POST /api/student/round/{round_id}/roommate Ask another student to be a roommate. rollNo: string DELETE /api/student/round/{round_id}/roommate Withdraw the roommate request. POST /api/student/roommate-requests/{request_id}/respond Accept or refuse a roommate request. accept: boolean GET /api/student/round/{round_id}/results Up to three chains for this student, best first. POST /api/student/round/{round_id}/chains/offer Offer a chain; it becomes a proposal with a three-day deadline. optionKind: string, chainNo: integer GET /api/student/proposals Proposals that include the student. POST /api/student/proposals/{proposal_id}/respond Accept or reject a proposal; one rejection ends it. accept: boolean

docs.title: Warden
docs.text:
Requires: A warden (admin) session.

Method Path Purpose Body / query GET /api/admin/hostels All hostels. GET /api/admin/hostels/{hostel_id}/round The hostel's latest round that is not cancelled. PUT /api/admin/hostels/{hostel_id}/room-types Declare how many rooms of a type the hostel has. roomType: string, quantity: integer GET /api/admin/hostels/{hostel_id}/room-types The hostel's declared room types. POST /api/admin/rounds Create a draft round for a hostel. hostelId: string POST /api/admin/rounds/{round_id}/open Open a draft round for registration. POST /api/admin/rounds/{round_id}/cancel Cancel a round; its open proposals are withdrawn. POST /api/admin/proposals/{proposal_id}/cancel Withdraw one proposal still collecting replies. POST /api/admin/rounds/{round_id}/lock-and-run Close registration and run the engine (k: Murty budget, max_chain: chain cap). k?, max_chain? GET /api/admin/rounds/{round_id}/summary Counts for the round: enrolled, chains, offers, executed. GET /api/admin/rounds/{round_id}/proposals Every proposal in the round with each member's reply.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Tutorial: Run a Swap Round End to End
docs.text: This walks one round from an empty database to a swap offer that every member must answer. It takes about ten minutes. Every account the seed scripts create uses the password swap1234.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/AakashChawla07/ucs503p-202627-hostel-swapping-service
cd ucs503p-202627-hostel-swapping-service
python -m venv .venv
.venv/Scripts/activate            # source .venv/bin/activate on Linux/macOS
pip install -e "./code[dev]"

docs.title: 2. Point it at a database
docs.text:
Any PostgreSQL 13 or later works: a local one, or a free Supabase project (Connect, then Session pooler, then copy the URI). Put the connection string in .env at the repository root:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname

Use a database of its own. The seed step below empties every table.

docs.title: 3. Create the tables and the demo hostel
docs.text:
python db/migrate.py     # applies db/migrations/0001, 0002, ...
python db/seed.py        # hostel A: 30 rooms, 30 students, warden admin001

docs.title: 4. Start the app
docs.text:
uvicorn hostelswap.api:app

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

docs.title: 5. Open a round (warden)
docs.text:
1. Sign in as admin001 / swap1234.
  2. Under Round control, press Create a round, then Open registration.

docs.title: 6. Fill the round with students
docs.text:
Students normally enrol and set their own priorities on the student page. To fill a round quickly, a script adds 28 enrolled students with priorities (roll numbers 1024030040 to 1024030067):

python db/seed_round.py

Reload the warden page: Enrolled and Priorities set read 28.

docs.title: 7. Run the matching (warden)
docs.text: Press Lock and run matching and keep the chain cap at 8. Locking closes registration for good, then the engine runs (Hungarian assignment, Murty's alternatives, cycles, the "nobody worse off" filter). The page then shows how many rings were found and how many students have at least one.

docs.title: 8. Offer a ring (student)
docs.text:
1. Log out, and sign in as a student, for example 1024030041.
  2. Your options lists up to three rings that include you, best for you first, with the match each member gets.
  3. Press Offer this swap on one, then Offer to N others. It becomes a proposal with a three-day deadline, and you have approved it already.

If a student has no options, try another roll number: not everyone is in a ring.

docs.title: 9. Answer it (the other members)
docs.text:
Sign in as each other member of the ring. Under Offers awaiting a reply they see the ring, everyone's reply so far and "closes in 3 d".

  • When the last member presses Accept, the swap executes: everyone moves, and the room history records the new allocations.
  • One Reject ends the ring at once and frees all its members.
  • If someone never answers, the ring expires after three days and its members are free to join another.

docs.title: 10. What the warden can do meanwhile
docs.text:
• Follow every ring and reply under Swap rings offered this round.
  • Withdraw a ring that is stuck; its students are freed.
  • Cancel round withdraws all of the round's open rings. Swaps that already executed stay.

docs.title: Without a database
docs.text:
With no DATABASE_URL, sign-in is unavailable, but the engine still runs on a built-in 30-student cohort: http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/demo?k=50. Compare k=1 with k=50: the same 77% satisfaction, but the longest chain falls from 28 students to 11.

See the API reference for every endpoint.

docs.title: Aabhas' Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024030673 Name: Aabhas Khandelwal

  • W2 : The app kept using the hardcoded data
  • W5 : CI could not install the package any more
  • W6 : The setup steps failed on a fresh clone

docs.title: Week 2 : The app kept using the hardcoded data
Problem
docs.text:
I moved our demo cohort into Supabase. The seed script ran fine:

seeded 30 students, 30 rooms in hostel A

The rows were there. I checked in the Supabase table editor - 30 students, 30 rooms, 90 preferences.

But the app showed exactly the same output as before, and the page still said:

data from hardcoded table

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
There were two different ways of finding the connection string.

The seed script reads .env itself, line by line. The app used os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL"), which only looks at the environment. Nothing loads .env into the environment, so:

seed script  -> reads .env    -> connects
web app      -> reads os.env  -> finds nothing -> falls back

The fallback made it worse. I had written it so a missing database means the app quietly serves the hardcoded cohort instead of crashing, so the demo cannot be killed by bad wifi. That is useful, but it also meant a broken configuration looked exactly like a working one.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
One place to look for the setting, checking both sources:

def dsn():
    from_env = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL")
    if from_env:
        return from_env
    if ENV_FILE.exists():
        # read DATABASE_URL out of .env
        ...
    return None

Then I made the fallback visible. The API returns where the data came from, and the page prints it:

data from postgres

I also added a log line, so the connection is visible while it happens:

INFO: connecting to postgres at db.xxxx.supabase.co
INFO: loaded 30 students, 30 rooms, 90 preferences from postgres

docs.title: Proof it is actually reading the database
docs.text:
I changed a name directly in Supabase and refreshed:

supabase : 1024030010  Aarav Sharma
renamed  -> app showed: PROOF FROM DATABASE
restored -> app showed: Aarav Sharma

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: A fallback that never fails is a fallback that hides mistakes. If the app can silently do something different from what I intended, it has to say which one it did. Adding the source field took two minutes and would have saved me the whole debugging session.

docs.title: Week 5 : CI could not install the package any more
Problem
docs.text: During the prototype-stage cleanup, pyproject.toml and requirements.txt were moved from the repo root into code/, next to the hostelswap package. My local environment was already installed, so nothing looked wrong there. But the tests workflow on GitHub installs the package fresh on every run, and that install step still pointed at the old location.

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
Two paths were still written relative to the old location.

The workflow installed from the repo root:

- name: Install
  run: pip install -e ".[dev]"

But the root no longer had a pyproject.toml, so pip had nothing to install.

Inside code/pyproject.toml, the wheel target still pointed at the old path, and readme pointed at a file that is not in code/:

readme = "README.md"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["code/hostelswap"]

Paths in pyproject.toml are relative to the file itself, so after the move code/hostelswap meant code/code/hostelswap.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Point the workflow at the new project folder, and make the package path relative to where pyproject.toml now lives:

run: pip install -e "./code[dev]"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["hostelswap"]

The readme line was dropped, since the README stays at the repo root.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
A fresh install from the new path, then the suite:

pip install -e "./code[dev]"
pytest -q
137 passed

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: Moving a config file moves every relative path inside it. When a file like pyproject.toml moves, the paths it names have to move with it, and the commands that point at it (CI, the README setup steps) have to be checked in the same commit.

docs.title: Week 6 : The setup steps failed on a fresh clone
Problem
docs.text:
After fixing CI for the pyproject.toml move, I followed our own README from scratch: clone, new virtual environment, install. The install failed straight away:

pip install -e ".[dev]"
ERROR: file:///.../c does not appear to be a Python project:
neither 'setup.py' nor 'pyproject.toml' found.

The docs site had the same command under "Running it".

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
When I fixed CI, I only changed the workflow. The same command was written in two more places that nobody runs automatically:

.github/workflows/tests.yml   pip install -e "./code[dev]"   <- fixed
README.md                     pip install -e ".[dev]"        <- stale
docs/index.md                 pip install -e ".[dev]"        <- stale

None of us noticed, because everyone in the team already had the package installed in an old environment. pytest -q kept passing on every laptop, while a new teammate or the evaluator would fail at the first step.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
The same one-line change in both files:

pip install -e "./code[dev]"

While updating the docs home page I also listed all three members, added a short status section, the frontend dev-server steps, and links to each member's journal.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
On a fresh clone in a temporary folder:

pip install -e ".[dev]"         -> ERROR, no pyproject.toml found
pip install -e "./code[dev]"    -> installs
pytest -q                       -> 137 passed

The docs site also builds with no warnings. My first link to the journals pointed at journals/, which has no index page and would have been a 404, so each member's journal is now linked directly.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: Setup instructions are code that is never tested. The only real check is the one a new person does: clone into an empty folder and follow the steps exactly. After any move of pyproject.toml, I now search the whole repo for the old command, not just the file that failed.

docs.title: Week 2 : The page showed nothing at all
Problem
docs.text:
The results page went completely blank. Not an error message, not half a table - a white screen.

The backend was fine. Opening the data directly in the browser worked:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/demo   ->  200, full JSON

So the data was there and the page still showed nothing.

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
The page gets the data and builds the whole table in one step:

const d = await (await fetch("/api/demo")).json();
out.innerHTML = `... ${d.chains.map(...)} ...`;

The backend response had changed, so d.chains did not exist any more. d.chains.map(...) failed, the function stopped right there, and out.innerHTML was never set. The page was left empty.

The error was only printed in the browser console, which I did not have open, so from the outside it just looked like nothing happened.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Check the response first, and show the problem if something is wrong:

try {
  const res = await fetch("/api/demo");
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("/api/demo returned " + res.status);
  d = await res.json();
} catch (err) {
  out.innerHTML = `<div class="err">Could not load the demo.<br>${err.message}</div>`;
  return;
}

Now a red box appears with the reason instead of a blank page.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
A blank page is the worst error message, because it looks the same whether the server is down, the data is wrong, or there is a typo in the JavaScript. A few lines turned it into a sentence saying what broke.

This matters for us because we demo this live. A red box telling us what to fix is recoverable in front of people. A white screen is not.

docs.title: Week 3 : The database rejected a value our code sends
Problem
docs.text:
We wrote the Postgres schema before the preference model was finished. A preference has a type, and we stored it as an enum:

create type criterion as enum (
    'hostel', 'floor', 'direction', 'washroom', 'room_type', 'roommate'
);

Later we added a new kind of preference: a student naming one specific room they want, with floor and direction as the fallbacks. In Python:

class Criterion(Enum):
    ROOM = "room"        # <- added later
    HOSTEL = "hostel"
    ...

The schema was never updated. Every one of our 30 demo students has a room preference, so the seed script would have failed on the very first insert:

invalid input value for enum criterion: "room"

docs.title: How we caught it
docs.text:
Before running the seed we compared the two lists directly, rather than running it and reading the error:

schema enum:  hostel, floor, direction, washroom, room_type, roommate
code sends:   room, floor, direction

room is in one list and not the other.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
The enum already existed in the live database, so we could not just edit schema.sql and re-run it. Postgres can add a value to an existing enum:

alter type criterion add value if not exists 'room' before 'hostel';

This is additive, so nothing already stored is affected. We also fixed schema.sql so a fresh setup gets it right the first time.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: An enum in the database is a copy of a list that also exists in the code, and nothing keeps the two in step. When we add a preference type we have to change it in both places, or the application will send a value the database has never heard of. A quick check comparing the two lists costs seconds and catches it before the insert fails.
